extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, playwrights, novelists, and other storytellers (writers seeking to design narrative for film and television)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on designing story for screen-based drama: principles of structure, events, scenes, beats, values, and the craft required to convert life into a meaningful, well-told story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign on the door reads 'Story Department.' A good story makes a good film possible, while failure to make the story work virtually guarantees disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story is the fundamental requirement; dialogue and description serve story. Writers who focus on dialogue/description but cannot make the story work waste their effort. Evaluate a work first on whether it tells a coherent, compelling story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common story problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, holes and other such story problems are root causes of bland, boring texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or revising, identify and fix progression gaps, ensure motivations are real and necessary, remove redundant characters, enrich subtext, and close narrative holes. These are primary failure modes to eliminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental story-design questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the total creative effort, most goes into designing story. Key questions: Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they go about getting it? What stops them? What are the consequences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist when conceiving or analyzing a story. Every major decision about events and structure should answer one or more of these questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer attitudes and loves
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer needs the love of story, the love of the dramatic, the love of truth, humanity, sensation, dreaming, humor, language, duality, perfection, uniqueness, beauty, and a love of self as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions/attitudes are prerequisites: they drive the search for meaningful material and sustain the arduous work of creation and revision. Assess whether the writer's commitment and sensibility align with these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is the sum total of means used to draw the audience into deep involvement, hold that involvement, and reward it with a moving and meaningful experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talent alone is not enough. The conscious mind must learn techniques of composition and revision so the subconscious can produce. Evaluate works for command of craft—structure, pacing, turning points, and the writer’s ability to rewrite toward perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'personal story' trap (understructured portraiture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'personal story' is understructured, a slice-of-life portrait that mistakes verisimilitude for truth; it reports facts but fails to reach Big-T Truth beneath the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware narratives that simply catalogue events because they 'actually happened.' Such stories lack depth and fail to abstract meaning from life. Revise to find the deeper organizing truth that the surface facts point to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'guaranteed commercial success' trap (spectacle overstory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'commercial' bad script is overstructured and overpopulated, mistaking spectacle (car chases, effects) for story; kinesis replaces imagination and lasts only briefly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle must be motivated by and subordinate to a strong story. Use technical innovations (e.g., CGI) to enrich story moments, not to substitute for meaningful conflict and human truth. Evaluate whether effects support the story or merely dazzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as metaphor for life (abstraction vs verbatim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller abstracts from life to discover essences; story must be like life but not verbatim. Fact is neutral; truth is what we think about what happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting real events or life details, select and shape them to express an interpretation or 'truth.' Ask whether choices deepen meaning rather than merely reporting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensory perception and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who lean to reportage often have the power of the senses; writers of action extravaganzas often have imaginative power. Strong storytelling strikes a balance along the spectrum between fact and imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate both sensorial acuity and imaginative leap—use concrete sensory detail and bold imagination in service of story. If writing drifts to one extreme, consciously draw in the complementary power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct talents: literary talent vs story talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary talent converts ordinary language into expressive form; story talent converts life into a clearer, more meaningful experience. Story talent is rarer and primary for film and TV, though literary talent is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a writer's strengths are literary (language, images) or story-driven (narrative shaping). Prioritize developing story talent for sustained success in screen storytelling and use craft to maximize literary gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as purposeful composition
rubrics_metrics.description: STRUCTURE is a selection of events from the characters' life stories composed into a strategic sequence to arouse specific emotions and to express a specific view of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure answers what to include/exclude and the order of events. Design choices must be driven by purpose: to arouse intended emotions and articulate ideas. Evaluate a work by how intentionally its events are sequenced toward a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Event: meaningful, value-charged, conflict-driven change
rubrics_metrics.description: A STORY EVENT creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character that is expressed and experienced in terms of a VALUE and achieved through CONFLICT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An event must affect a character, be framed by a value (alive/dead, love/hate, etc.), and arise from struggle. Coincidence alone (e.g., rain by chance) is insufficient; events should emerge from character and conflict to be meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Values
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY VALUES are the universal qualities of human experience that may shift from positive to negative or negative to positive (e.g., love/hate, freedom/slavery, hope/despair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use binary, reversible values to charge events and scenes. When analyzing a scene/event, identify the value at stake and how it shifts. Values are the soul of storytelling—choose and manipulate them deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene must turn a value (definition of scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: A SCENE is an action through conflict in more or less continuous time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character’s life on at least one value with a degree of perceptible significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally every scene is a story event. If the opening and closing value of a scene are the same, the scene is a nonevent—likely exposition—and should be cut or its information woven elsewhere. Use the 'turn test' for every scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: No scene that doesn't turn
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no scene that does not change the value-charged condition of a character’s life from beginning to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a scene's value state is unchanged, question its inclusion. Many such scenes are merely expository and can be eliminated or their necessary information integrated into turning scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat as smallest structural unit
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is an exchange of behavior in action/reaction. Beat by beat these changing behaviors shape the turning of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze scenes in terms of beats—distinct behavior exchanges that incrementally change direction toward the scene's turning point. Use beats to sculpt pacing and causal progression within scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence definition and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene; the capping scene of a sequence delivers a more powerful, determinant change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange scenes into sequences that escalate stakes and culminate in determinant changes. Plan sequences so their final scene delivers a stronger shift than the preceding scenes, creating momentum and structural hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical film scene count guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: For a typical film, the writer will choose forty to sixty Story Events or scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a planning guideline: aim for roughly 40–60 scenes/events in a feature, fewer for plays, more for novels. Scene quantity should serve structure and pacing, not be an arbitrary goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical scene-testing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When auditing a scene, note the value at the top and the close of the scene. If the value is unchanged, ask: Why is this scene in my script?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make literal notes of opening/closing value-charges for each scene during revision. Use this test to identify nonevents and prioritize rewrites that ensure each scene contributes meaningful change.
